HR@10 with one positive and 99 sampled negatives measures ranking within 100 candidates; it does not establish full-catalog top-10 quality. Krichene and Rendle show that sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation. Keep the pinned evaluator unchanged, but describe gains specifically as sampled-candidate validation gains. Fixed candidates support paired comparisons; they do not remove sampling bias. [On Sampled Metrics](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/).

For uncertainty, a practical application of paired bootstrap is to retain each model’s per-user hit indicator, resample the same user indices for both models within each category, and recompute the four-category macro-average difference. Report that difference with a 95% interval and category-level changes. With 200 users/category, one additional hit changes category HR by 0.5 percentage points and macro HR by 0.125 points. This bootstrap requires no retraining; it estimates user-sampling uncertainty conditional on the fitted models and fixed candidates, excluding training-seed and candidate-resampling variability. [SciPy paired bootstrap](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.bootstrap.html).

Repeatedly choosing architectures or checkpoints on the same validation users introduces selection optimism: the best observed result partly reflects favorable noise. Ordinary paired confidence intervals do not correct this adaptive selection. Record the number of comparisons, predefine checkpoint selection where possible, and treat small winning margins as provisional until the host’s separate held-out evaluation. An interval spanning zero indicates inconclusive evidence, not equivalence. [Cawley and Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html).
